blocks.markdown: Definition and acquisition: Sections 121.1–122

**Mark (Sec. 121.1).** Any visible sign capable of distinguishing the goods (trademark) or services (service mark) of an enterprise, including a stamped or marked container of goods. A mark distinguishes commercial source: trademark for goods, service mark for services.
Rights in a mark are acquired through registration validly made under the law — valid registration is the statutory mode of acquisition.
Registrability: spectrum of distinctiveness and Section 123

Spectrum of distinctiveness (study taxonomy, not a separate Code section): fanciful, arbitrary, suggestive, descriptive, generic. Fanciful, arbitrary and suggestive marks are ordinarily inherently distinctive; descriptive marks may need acquired distinctiveness where permitted; generic terms are not registrable for the goods or services they name.

A mark cannot be registered if it: (a) is immoral, deceptive or scandalous, or disparaging; (b) uses Philippine or foreign flags, coats of arms or insignia; (c) identifies a living individual (or a deceased President's widow during her life) without written consent; (d) is identical with a registered or earlier-filed mark for the same, closely related, or confusingly nearly resembling goods/services; (e)–(f) is identical with, confusingly similar to, or a translation of a well-known mark; (g) is likely to mislead the public; (h)–(j) consists exclusively of generic, customary, or descriptive signs; (k) is a technically or functionally necessitated shape; (l) is color alone undefined by form; or (m) is contrary to public order or morality. Match the mark to the specific statutory bar.
Similar marks: confusion and the dominancy test

Two types of confusion: confusion of goods (the purchaser buys one product believing it is the other) and confusion of business or source (the purchaser believes different goods or services come from, are connected with, or are sponsored by the same source). Likelihood of confusion may concern either; actual confusion is not required.

Section 123.1(e) covers identical, confusingly similar, or translated well-known marks used for identical or similar goods or services — well-knownness is judged by knowledge among the relevant sector of the public, including knowledge obtained through promotion, not the public at large. Section 123.1(f) extends protection to dissimilar goods or services where use would indicate a connection with the registered owner and the owner's interests are likely to be damaged.

**Current similarity test: dominancy.** The holistic test has been abandoned by the Kolin en banc Court. Compare dominant features and the marks' visual, aural and connotative impressions, with the ordinary purchaser, relatedness of goods, and normal potential expansion of business in mind.
Application, duration, renewal and cancellation

The Filipino-or-English application must contain: (a) request for registration; (b) applicant name and address; (c) nationality, domicile and establishment; (d) organizing law for juridical persons; (e) agent or representative if not domiciled here; (f) priority claim; (g) color claim; (h) three-dimensional statement; (i) reproductions; (j) transliteration or translation; (k) goods/services grouped by Nice classes; and (l) applicant or representative signature or self-identification. Keep the representation of the mark and the classes clear.

After the opposition period expires or the Director of Legal Affairs denies the opposition, the Office issues the certificate of registration on payment of the fee, with notice published in the IPO Gazette.

A certificate of registration is prima facie evidence of the registration's validity, the registrant's ownership, and the exclusive right to use the mark for the specified goods/services and related goods/services. Prima facie evidence is rebuttable, not conclusive in every dispute.

A certificate remains in force for ten years, but the registrant must file a declaration of actual use with evidence — or show valid reasons based on obstacles to use — within one year from the fifth anniversary of registration; otherwise the mark is removed from the Register.

Registration may be renewed for successive ten-year periods on payment of the fee and filing of a request — made within six months before expiration, or within six months after expiration on payment of the additional fee.

A person who believes he is or will be damaged may petition for cancellation within five years from registration. At any time, cancellation may be sought where the mark has become generic, is abandoned, was obtained fraudulently or contrary to the Act, misrepresents source, or has not been used in the Philippines for an uninterrupted three years or longer without legitimate reason. The section also governs jurisdiction where an enforcement suit or cancellation petition has been filed.

Non-use may be excused only if caused by circumstances arising independently of the owner's will — lack of funds does not excuse non-use. Use in a form not altering distinctive character is not a ground for cancellation; use on one or more goods/services in a class may prevent cancellation for the others; and qualifying use by a related company or controlled user may inure to the registrant subject to statutory conditions.
Rights conferred: Section 147

The registered owner may prevent unauthorized third-party commercial use of identical or similar signs or containers for identical or similar goods/services where use would likely confuse. Use of an identical sign for identical goods/services carries a presumption of confusion. A registered well-known mark's protection extends to dissimilar goods/services if use would indicate a connection with the owner and the owner's interests are likely to be damaged.
Infringement: Sections 155–156

Section 155 describes the infringing conduct (Section 156, listed in the syllabus, deals primarily with remedies). Without the owner's consent, it is infringement to: (155.1) use in commerce a reproduction, counterfeit, copy or colorable imitation of a registered mark, the same container, or a dominant feature, in connection with sale, offering, distribution or advertising — including preparatory steps — where use is likely to cause confusion, mistake or deception; or (155.2) reproduce, counterfeit, copy or colorably imitate the mark or a dominant feature and apply it to labels, signs, prints, packages, wrappers, receptacles or advertisements for commerce where use is likely to confuse. Infringement occurs on commission of either act, regardless of whether there is an actual sale.

The owner may recover damages measured by the profit the complainant would have made, the profit the defendant actually made, or — if neither is readily ascertainable — a reasonable percentage of gross sales or service value. The court may impound sales invoices and documents during the action, double damages on shown actual intent to mislead or defraud, and grant an injunction on proper showing.
Unfair competition: Section 168

One who has identified his goods, business or services in the public mind — whether or not with a registered mark — has a property right in that goodwill. Unfair competition is employing deception or other means contrary to good faith to pass off one's goods, business or services as another's, or committing acts calculated to produce that result. Deemed unfair competition: (a) selling goods with the general appearance of another's goods (wrapping, packages, devices, words, features) likely to make purchasers believe they are another's; (b) artifice inducing false belief that one offers another's services; or (c) false trade statements or other bad-faith acts discrediting another's goods, business or services. Sections 156, 157 and 161 remedies apply mutatis mutandis. The key inquiry differs from infringement: deceptive general appearance and intent to deceive or defraud.

table.caption: Trademark infringement vs unfair competition
rows: The registered mark or its dominant feature.
Goodwill identified in the public mind, even without a registered mark.
Unauthorized commercial use likely to cause confusion, mistake or deception.
Passing off through deception or bad-faith means; deceptive general appearance.
Likelihood of confusion suffices; actual intent only aggravates damages.
Intent to deceive the public and defraud a competitor, inferable from circumstances.

blocks.markdown: **Case recitation format.** Facts: only what matters to the syllabus rule. Issue: a yes-or-no question tied to the provision or doctrine. Ruling: the disposition and decisive reason in plain language. Doctrine: the reusable rule, plus a short exact phrase only when verified.
